lesson.title: Isolating What You're Testing: Explanatory Factors in an Experiment
lesson.summary: A factor is an explanatory variable an experimenter deliberately manipulates, and studying two or more factors together in one experiment lets researchers detect interactions that a single-factor experiment could never reveal.
lesson.body:
A factor is an explanatory variable that an experimenter deliberately manipulates in order to study its effect on a response variable. When an experiment involves only one thing being varied, such as fertilizer type in the earlier example, that one variable is the experiment's single factor. Many real experiments manipulate more than one factor at a time, which is what lets researchers study several questions in a single, efficient study.

A treatment, as defined in the previous section, is the specific combination of factor levels a unit actually receives. When there is only one factor, treatment and factor level are essentially the same thing. Once an experiment has two or more factors, a treatment becomes a pairing: one level of the first factor together with one level of the second factor, and so on for however many factors are being studied.

Suppose researchers now want to know how both fertilizer amount and watering frequency affect corn yield. Fertilizer amount is one factor and watering frequency is a second factor. If fertilizer amount is tested at two levels, low and high, and watering frequency is tested at two levels, daily and every other day, there are four possible treatments formed by combining one level of each factor: low fertilizer with daily watering, low fertilizer with every-other-day watering, high fertilizer with daily watering, and high fertilizer with every-other-day watering. If 8 plots are randomly assigned to each of these four treatment combinations, that is 32 plots total, and researchers can measure not only whether fertilizer matters and whether watering matters, but also whether the two factors interact, meaning the effect of one depends on the level of the other.

Studying two factors together in one experiment is far more efficient than running two separate single-factor experiments, because every plot contributes information about both factors simultaneously, and because interactions between factors, which single-factor experiments cannot detect at all, often matter enormously in practice. A fertilizer that works wonderfully with daily watering might do nothing under infrequent watering, a pattern that only a multi-factor experiment can reveal.

An interaction is easiest to see with numbers. Suppose the average yields for the four treatment combinations turn out to be 140 bushels per acre for low fertilizer with daily watering, 148 for low fertilizer with every-other-day watering, 155 for high fertilizer with daily watering, and 171 for high fertilizer with every-other-day watering. Moving from low to high fertilizer raises yield by 15 bushels under daily watering, 155 minus 140, but by 23 bushels under every-other-day watering, 171 minus 148. Fertilizer's effect depends on the watering level, exactly the kind of factor-by-factor interaction a single-factor experiment could never have exposed.

The specific values a factor is tested at, low and high fertilizer, daily and every-other-day watering, are called the levels of the factor. Choosing how many levels to test and what those levels should be is its own important design decision, covered next.
